title: Supervised Fine-Tuning & Instruction Following
oneLineScope: Taking a pretrained base language model and continuing its training on curated instruction–response demonstrations — the step that turns a text predictor into an instruction follower.
prose:
A pretrained language model — GPT-3, say, at 175B parameters — is a sophisticated text predictor. Ask it a direct question and it may answer you, or it may continue the question with another question, or produce a plausible-looking follow-on sentence that is orthogonal to your intent. This is not a failure of intelligence; it is the faithful consequence of what the model was trained to do: assign high probability to the next token in text drawn from the web. The web does not consist primarily of helpful question–answer exchanges. Supervised fine-tuning — sometimes called instruction-tuning — is the step that bridges the gap between “predict the next token as it typically appears” and “do what this instruction says.”

The process

Take a pretrained base model with parameters \(\theta_0\). Construct, or curate, a dataset of \((\text{instruction},\, \text{response})\) pairs — demonstrations of the behavior you want. The instruction might be a question, a translation request, a summarization prompt, a coding task; the response is the answer or completion a competent person would produce. Then continue training the model on that dataset with the exact same objective as pretraining: minimize the average negative log-likelihood of the response tokens given the instruction tokens,

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t} \log P_{\theta}(r_t \mid \text{instruction},\, r_1, \ldots, r_{t-1}) \]

where \(r_1, \ldots, r_T\) are the response tokens, and the loss is computed only over the response (not the instruction). The machinery is unchanged — next-token cross-entropy, the same optimizer, the same weight update rule. The only difference from pretraining is the data distribution: instead of a large sample of naturally occurring text, the training corpus is a curated set of instruction–response demonstrations representing the behavior the deployer wants.

The result is a model \(\theta^{\prime}\) that has been nudged from its pretraining distribution toward the instruction-following distribution. It has learned, through the loss, that when an instruction appears in the context, the appropriate continuation is a responsive and helpful answer — not a Wikipedia-style continuation, not another question, not a tangential paragraph.

FLAN and InstructGPT

Two papers established the canonical pattern. Wei et al. (2021) introduced FLAN (Finetuned Language Models are Zero-Shot Learners): they took a 137B parameter LM and fine-tuned it on a mixture of over 60 NLP tasks, each phrased as a natural-language instruction. The key finding was that instruction-tuning on a diverse enough mixture of tasks dramatically improved zero-shot generalization to held-out tasks the model had never seen in any form — including tasks not represented in the fine-tuning mix. The breadth of tasks during SFT seems to teach the model something general about the instruction-following format, not just narrow task-specific behaviors.

Ouyang et al. (2022) described InstructGPT, whose first stage is supervised fine-tuning of exactly this kind: human contractors write high-quality prompt–response demonstrations, the base GPT-3 model is fine-tuned on them with cross-entropy, and the resulting model already follows instructions substantially better than the raw pretrained base. InstructGPT then continues with a second stage — reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) — but the SFT stage is a prerequisite and makes that second stage tractable.

Where this leads

Supervised fine-tuning transforms the pretraining investment into a product. The base model's knowledge — everything learned from hundreds of billions of tokens — is already in the weights; SFT redirects the model's output behavior toward producing it helpfully. RLHF then refines that behavior further using human preference comparisons rather than demonstrations. That step is where the story continues, and it is explicitly out of scope here: RLHF involves a reward model trained on pairwise human rankings, a policy optimization loop, and a body of alignment literature that deserves its own treatment. The present node closes at the SFT boundary — a genuinely useful instruction follower, obtained by the simplest possible means: supervised learning on demonstrations.

bibliography.citation: Wei, J., et al. (2021). "Finetuned Language Models are Zero-Shot Learners." ICLR 2022.
bibliography.annotation: The FLAN paper. §3 describes the instruction-tuning setup: 62 tasks rephrased as natural-language instructions, fine-tuned on a 137B LM. §4 reports the zero-shot generalization improvement on held-out task clusters. The clearest demonstration that broad instruction-tuning teaches a general capability, not narrow task memorization. Read §2–4 for the core result.

bibliography.citation: Ouyang, L., et al. (2022). "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback." NeurIPS 35.
bibliography.annotation: The InstructGPT paper. §3.1 describes the SFT stage: human contractor demonstrations, cross-entropy fine-tuning of GPT-3. §3.2–3.3 describe the subsequent RLHF stages — those are out of scope here but useful to scan to understand why SFT alone is not the end of the story. §4 gives the human-evaluation results comparing SFT, RLHF, and the raw base model.

bibliography.citation: Liang, P., et al. (2022). "Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM)." TMLR.
bibliography.annotation: Benchmarks instruction-following models (including InstructGPT variants) on a wide range of tasks with consistent evaluation methodology. Useful for seeing what SFT-trained models can and cannot do in practice, and for calibrating claims about the generalization benefit of instruction-tuning. §4–5 cover the evaluation dimensions most relevant here.
